pageInfo.subtitle: Learn to target chord tones for melodic, intentional solos that outline the harmony.
pageInfo.heroDescription: The secret to great solos isn't just knowing scales - it's knowing which notes in those scales matter most over each chord. Chord tone soloing teaches you to target the root, 3rd, 5th, and 7th of each chord, creating melodies that follow the harmony and sound intentional rather than random.

items.text: Chord tones are the strongest notes to land on over any chord
The 3rd defines major vs minor - the most important chord tone to target
Use scale tones to connect between chord tones
Land on chord tones on strong beats (1 and 3)
Start by playing only chord tones (arpeggios) over changes
Then add passing tones (scale notes) between chord tones
Practice with backing tracks to hear the effect
Visualize chord shapes under your scale patterns

exercises.title: Root Note Targeting
exercises.description: Over a C-Am-F-G progression, play freely from the C major scale but always land on the ROOT note of each chord on beat 1. This builds awareness of where root notes sit within scale patterns.

notation.title: Root Note Targeting over I-vi-IV-V
notation.staveTitle: Landing on Root of Each Chord

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: The root notes for C-Am-F-G are C(8th fret 6th string), A(5th fret 6th string), F(1st fret 6th string), G(3rd fret 6th string). Always know where the root is before the chord changes.

exercises.title: 3rd Targeting - Major vs Minor
exercises.description: Over the same C-Am-F-G progression, target the 3RD of each chord on beat 1. The 3rd is the most colorful chord tone - it defines whether the chord is major or minor. C's 3rd is E, Am's 3rd is C, F's 3rd is A, G's 3rd is B.

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: This is the single most transformative chord tone skill. When you target the 3rd, your solo outlines the chord quality. Listeners hear you 'following the changes' even if subconsciously.

exercises.title: Full Arpeggio Outlines
exercises.description: Play the full arpeggio (root-3rd-5th) of each chord as quarter notes. This gives you the raw chord tone vocabulary. Once comfortable, add passing tones between arpeggio notes.

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Visualize the chord shape on the fretboard. The arpeggio notes are hidden within the chord shape. CAGED system knowledge helps you find chord tones in every position.

exercises.title: Approach Notes
exercises.description: Approach each chord tone from one fret below (chromatic approach) or from the scale note above (diatonic approach). This technique creates tension and resolution that sounds sophisticated and intentional.

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: Chromatic approaches create momentary tension that resolves beautifully to the chord tone. Jazz players use this extensively. Start simply: one approach note into one chord tone per chord.

exercises.title: Blues Chord Tone Soloing
exercises.description: Over a 12-bar blues in A (A7-D7-E7), target chord tones while using the minor pentatonic scale for passing tones. On A7 target A-C#-E-G, on D7 target D-F#-A-C, on E7 target E-G#-B-D.

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: The magic of blues chord tone soloing is mixing the minor pentatonic scale (for feel) with the major 3rd of each chord (for harmonic accuracy). Hitting the 3rd of each dominant chord is what makes blues solos shine.

exercises.title: ii-V-I Chord Tone Navigation
exercises.description: Over a Dm7-G7-Cmaj7 progression (ii-V-I in C major), outline each chord's arpeggio: Dm7(D-F-A-C), G7(G-B-D-F), Cmaj7(C-E-G-B). Notice how common tones connect the chords.

practiceNotes.title: Practice Notes
practiceNotes.text: The ii-V-I is the most common progression in jazz. Notice shared tones: Dm7 and G7 share D, G7 and Cmaj7 share B. Use these common tones as pivot points between chord changes.

items.title: Building Melodic Solos
items: Think melody first, speed second - great solos are singable
Chord tones on strong beats, scale tones on weak beats
The 7th of one chord often resolves to the 3rd of the next
Visualize the chord shape under your fingers even during scale runs

items.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid
items: Running scales without targeting any specific notes over chord changes
Playing the same licks regardless of the underlying harmony
Ignoring the 3rd - the most defining chord tone
Never practicing over actual chord progressions (use backing tracks)
